title: Shred
goal: Alternate, economy, legato, sweeps and tapping in A minor, built up one technique at a time, finishing with an eight-bar sixteenth-note run over a band at 100 BPM.
assumes: You can play the A minor pentatonic box at fret 5 and eighth notes with a click at 90 BPM. No speed is assumed. The minutes are one pass through the material; the drills are meant to be repeated for weeks, and their variants change keys and strings so the repetition stays fresh.

skills: Eighth notes with a click at 90 BPM

orderRationale: The teacher's fifteen-Step outline, in its order: one string, then accents and groupings, then four-finger independence, then crossings, so that by Step 5 every later technique has its parts. The Path rotates techniques instead of finishing one before the next, because a shredder needs them together and because a rotation keeps a daily Session from being one drill. Picking comes first and stays the backbone: economy picking (Step 10) is taught only after strict alternate picking is reliable across strings and skips, so it is a choice and not a crutch. Legato and sweeps come late because both lean on a fretting hand built by the chromatic Step, and because the app can grade them least: legato is tied to picked notes, and sweeps say 'timing only' in their titles. Tapping and the eight-bar run close it. Where it departs from the outline: Step 1 adds Alternate Picking's 'four of each' as a fourth graded Exercise, Step 6 lands the six-note licks on a quarter note so they stay in sixteenths, Step 10 keeps the alternate-picked arpeggios beside the economy ones for contrast, and every legato Exercise is a picked bar followed by the same notes legato.
gradingLimits: Picked single notes, sixteenths to about 120 BPM and sextuplets to about 90, are the case the app is built for: timing evenness, notes heard and extra notes, plus right notes where the notes are at least 75 ms apart and the pitch is clear, after the take. None of it has been tried on a real guitar. Legato: a hammer-on or pull-off the app doesn't hear costs nothing, so the timing leans on the picked notes and the volume of the legato notes is a self-check; a hammer-on from nowhere and a tap count as attacks that must be heard. Sweeps are graded on timing only: swept notes ring into each other, right notes mostly read 'not checked', and their titles say so; only rungs with at least 150 ms between notes are graded. Accents are rough, louder or not. Pick direction is never heard: it is a checklist item wherever the strokes matter. Above sixteenths at 100 BPM, read the timing as provisional until the input delay is calibrated, and use a clean or light-crunch tone for graded takes.

steps.title: One-string sixteenths
steps.goal: Four notes to every click on one string, even, at 110 to 120 BPM.
steps.why: Every fast line in this Path is this motion with something added: a crossing, a shape, a legato note. On one string there is nothing to hide behind, so an uneven stroke shows up at once, and it is the cheapest place to fix it. Sixteenths at 110 to 120 is where most players' picking either becomes a motion they trust or starts to lock up.
howTo: Count '1 e and a': down on 1 and 'and', up on 'e' and 'a'. Every Exercise in this Step is sixteenth notes, four to each click.
Pick from the wrist, small. If the forearm locks, drop one rung: the locked arm is the usual speed wall, not the fingers.
Keep down and up strokes the same loudness. Uneven pick depth is the most common reason they are not.
steps.payoff: Two bars of open-string sixteenths that sound like a machine, and a one-string lick at fret 12 that already sounds like shred.

exercises.title: Open A, sixteenths
exercises.purpose: Take the fretting hand out of it, so the only question is whether every stroke lands on its sixteenth.
howTo: Sixteenth notes on the open A string, strictly down-up, for eight bars. Rest the picking hand lightly on the bridge so the low E stays quiet.
exercises.coachLine: This one is only about time. I'll say how even the eight bars were and whether any note went missing.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: The fret-12 loop: 12-13-15-13
exercises.purpose: A one-string loop high on the neck, the kind of figure a shredder repeats for a whole bar. Three fingers, one string, the pick never stops.
howTo: Sixteenths. First finger on fret 12, second on 13, little finger on 15, then back to 13. Repeat without a break; the 13 leads back into the 12.
Leave the first finger down while the others play, so it is already there for the next loop.
exercises.coachLine: Evenness first, then the notes. I'll check both after the take.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: 1-2-3-4 on the G string
exercises.purpose: All four fingers, one per fret, at sixteenths: the fingers have to land exactly when the pick does.
howTo: Sixteenths. Bar 1: frets 5, 6, 7, 8 with fingers 1, 2, 3, 4, four times. Bar 2: move the hand up one fret and come down 9, 8, 7, 6 with 4, 3, 2, 1.
Keep each finger down until the next one lands. If the notes come out as flams, the fingers are running ahead of the pick: make them lazier.
exercises.coachLine: If the notes bunch up, drop one rung. I'll check the notes and the timing after the take.

exercises.title: Four of each, on the top string
exercises.purpose: A melody where the fretting hand moves once a beat and the pick never stops: the rate in the right hand, the music in the left.
howTo: Sixteenths, four per note, on the top string: A, C, B, A, then G, A, B, C. Move the fretting hand exactly on the beat, not a hair before.
This is tremolo picking in slow motion, and a good first thing to play on any day.
exercises.coachLine: Four notes per pitch makes the time easy to judge, and I'll check the notes after the take.

steps.title: Accents and groupings
steps.goal: Put the accent where the music wants it, on a downstroke or an upstroke, in sextuplets and across the beat, without the time moving.
steps.why: Fast playing is heard in groups, not notes: a run of sextuplets sounds like shred only when the first of every six is stronger. Accents also prove the picking hand is under control rather than running on its own, and an accent on an upstroke is the honest test of that.
howTo: An accent is a little more depth and speed in one stroke. Don't squeeze, and keep the unaccented notes quiet on purpose: the contrast makes the accent.
Sextuplets are six notes to the click, two groups of three: say 'one-trip-let-two-trip-let'. Sixteenths are four to the click.
Use a clean or light-crunch tone. Compression and high gain flatten accents, for your ear and for the app.
steps.payoff: The same notes that sounded like a typewriter now have a pulse, and a six-note figure rolls against the beat the way it does on the records.

exercises.title: 8-7-5-7-8-7 in sextuplets, accent on the beat
exercises.purpose: The classic six-note one-string figure, with the first of every six marked so you hear the beat inside the blur.
howTo: Sextuplets, six to the click, on the top string: frets 8, 7, 5, 7, 8, 7 with fingers 4, 3, 1, 3, 4, 3. Accent the first note of each six.
Six is even, so every group starts on a downstroke and the accent is always a downstroke here.
exercises.coachLine: Accent checks are rough: I can only tell louder from not louder. Evenness and missed notes are firmer.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.
Accents are measured roughly, as louder than the notes either side. Compression and high gain flatten them.

exercises.title: The same six as sixteenths: three against four
exercises.purpose: The six notes again, now four to the click, with an accent every three notes. The accents walk across the beat and fall on upstrokes half the time.
howTo: Sixteenths. Frets 8, 7, 5, 7, 8, 7 on the top string, accents on the first and fourth note of each six: the 8 and the second 7. That is an accent every three sixteenths, so the pattern takes three bars to come back to beat 1.
Tap your foot on the click, not on the accents, and let the two disagree.
exercises.coachLine: Your accents should fall against the click here, which makes it a good one to listen back to.

exercises.title: Sixteenth triplets on open A, accent every third
exercises.purpose: Six to the click on one open string, with the accent on every third note, so it lands on a downstroke, then an upstroke, then a downstroke.
howTo: Sextuplets (sixteenth triplets), six to the click, on the open A string. Accent notes 1 and 4 of each six: the first is a downstroke, the second an upstroke.
If only the downstroke accents come out, dig the upstroke a little deeper rather than hitting the downstroke softer.
exercises.coachLine: Accent checks are rough. If the upstroke accents disappear on the recording, that is the thing to work on.

Accents are measured roughly, as louder than the notes either side. Compression and high gain flatten them.

exercises.title: Walk the accent through the beat
exercises.purpose: One note, four bars, and the accent moves from the first sixteenth to the last. Bars 2 and 4 put it on an upstroke.
howTo: Sixteenths on fret 7 of the G string. Bar 1 accents the first of each four, bar 2 the second, bar 3 the third, bar 4 the fourth. Keep the time dead still at each change.
exercises.coachLine: Bars 2 and 4 are the test. The accent reading is rough, so trust your ear too.

steps.difficultyException: The tempo drops on purpose: an accent is a control problem, and the note-rate metric only counts speed.

steps.title: Petrucci chromatic and the spider
steps.goal: One finger per fret across all six strings, even at sixteenths, with the hand moving up the neck.
steps.why: Chromatic drills are not music, and that is why they work: there is no tune to carry you, so every weak finger and every awkward string change is exposed. Ten minutes of this a day is the classic way to make the fourth finger as useful as the first and to make string changes stop being events.
howTo: One finger per fret: first finger on the lowest fret of the four, little finger on the highest. Keep the fingers close to the strings, curved, tips down.
Sixteenths throughout, four to the click.
Thumb behind the neck, relaxed. If it squeezes, the little finger tires first.
Stop at any pain in the hand, wrist or forearm. A tired forearm is one thing and pain is another; pain ends the set.
steps.payoff: Your little finger keeps up, and a six-string crawl that used to stumble at the B string now sounds like one line.

exercises.title: 1-2-3-4 across six strings, up a fret each pass
exercises.purpose: Up all six strings at fret 5, move up a fret, come back down; up at fret 7, down at fret 8. The whole fretting hand works, and it shifts.
howTo: Sixteenths. Bar 1 and a half: 1-2-3-4 on each string from the low E to the top E, starting at fret 5. Then shift up one fret and play 4-3-2-1 on each string from the top E down.
Shift during the last note of a pass, not after it. Six bars, then it starts again.
exercises.coachLine: Long lines are where the time drifts. I'll report evenness over the whole take and the notes after it.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

notPooled.reason: The frets get wider toward the nut, so a low start is harder than a high one.

exercises.title: The spider: 1-3 then 2-4 on a pair of strings
exercises.purpose: Two fingers on one string while two work on the next, so the fingers move in pairs and never all at once. It is the best cure there is for a hand that collapses.
howTo: Sixteenths, a pair of strings to each beat. On the low E and A: finger 1 at fret 5 on the E, finger 3 at fret 7 on the A, then finger 2 at fret 6 on the E, finger 4 at fret 8 on the A.
Bar 1 crawls up a string pair each beat (E-A, A-D, D-G, G-B); bar 2 goes on to B-E and crawls back (G-B, D-G, A-D).
Lift each finger only when its partner on the other string has landed.
exercises.coachLine: This is a diagnostic, so play it slowly enough to hear the weakest change. I'll check the timing and the notes.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: The 1-3-2-4 permutation
exercises.purpose: The same four fingers in a crossed order, so no finger can lean on its neighbour. It is harder than it looks and it shows exactly which finger is weak.
howTo: Sixteenths. Up: frets 5, 7, 6, 8 (fingers 1, 3, 2, 4) on each string from the low E to the top. Then shift up a fret and come down with 4-2-3-1: frets 9, 7, 8, 6 on each string from the top E.
Say the finger numbers out loud for the first few passes.
exercises.coachLine: Stay on a rung that keeps it even. Fast and rough teaches the wrong thing here.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

steps.title: Crossing two strings
steps.goal: Change strings at sixteenths with no gap and no scrape, on both kinds of crossing.
steps.why: On one string the pick has nothing in its way; between two strings it has to get over one of them. There are only two kinds of crossing, and every line in the rest of this Path is built from them: outside, where the pick travels around the pair, and inside, where it is trapped between the strings and has to escape.
howTo: Outside: a downstroke on the lower-pitched string, then an upstroke on the higher one. Each stroke starts from outside the pair.
Inside: an upstroke on the lower-pitched string, then a downstroke on the higher one. Each stroke starts between the two strings, so the pick must hop out of the gap.
Much of this motion is a small tilt of the wrist. Try it slowly with no click first, then sixteenths with the click.
steps.payoff: A short A minor lick that used to trip every time now rolls, and you can name which crossing is the one that catches you.

exercises.title: Outside pairs on G and B
exercises.purpose: Moving pairs of notes, all outside crossings, so the fretting hand gets busier while the pick path never changes.
howTo: Sixteenths. Two of each pair, then change: C and E, D and G, C and F, D and E. The strokes never change: down on the G string, up on the B string.
exercises.coachLine: I can time these and check the notes. Which way the pick went is yours to keep honest, so the checklist asks.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: Watch the pick for one pass, or film it: was every G-string note a downstroke and every B-string note an upstroke?

exercises.title: Inside pairs on B and G
exercises.purpose: The same four pairs, top note first, so every crossing is inside. Compare it honestly with the outside take.
howTo: Sixteenths. Down on the B string, up on the G string. If you hear a tiny gap at each change, that is the hop out of the strings: make it smaller.
exercises.coachLine: Compare this take with the outside one. The gap between the two is what you are working on.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: Watch the pick for one pass: was every B-string note a downstroke and every G-string note an upstroke?

exercises.title: The all-outside A minor lick
exercises.purpose: Eight notes that sound like a real pentatonic lick and happen to contain only outside crossings. This is the Step's payoff.
howTo: Sixteenths, the lick twice a bar: A on the D string, C and D on the G string, E on the B string, back down D and C, then A and G on the D string.
Start on a downstroke on the D string. Every string change works out as outside; keep it that way by never adding a stroke.
exercises.coachLine: This is music now. Get it even, then take it up one rung at a time.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: Was the first note of every lick a downstroke on the D string?

steps.title: Gilbert pentatonic crossings
steps.goal: Loop a two-string pentatonic figure in sextuplets, then move it down the box, without the crossing ever catching.
steps.why: Two notes on each of two strings, looped, is the figure behind a great deal of fast rock soloing: it sounds wild and is only four frets. It is also the purest inside-crossing drill there is, because every string change in the six-note loop is inside. Learn it here and the pentatonic box stops being something you walk through and becomes something you can play fast.
howTo: The box is A minor pentatonic at fret 5: first finger on fret 5, third or little finger on the upper note of each string.
Sextuplets: six to the click. The six-note loop fills one beat exactly, so the loop starts on every click.
Keep the crossings small. The pick only has to clear one string; most of the miss comes from swinging too wide.
steps.payoff: A blurring pentatonic loop at a tempo you can play in a solo, and the same loop on any pair of strings in the box.

exercises.title: The six-note loop on B and E
exercises.purpose: E, G on the B string, A, C, A on the top string, G again: six notes, all inside crossings, looped.
howTo: Sextuplets. B string fret 5 then 8, top string 5, 8, 5, then B string 8, and round again from the B string's 5.
Down, up, down, up, down, up: six is even, so every loop starts on a downstroke.
exercises.coachLine: This is the corner that long runs trip on. Evenness tells the story, and I'll check the notes after.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: The same loop down the box
exercises.purpose: One loop on each pair of strings: B and E, G and B, D and G, A and D, then back up. The pick path is the same; the fretting hand has to find each pair in time.
howTo: Sextuplets, one loop to a beat. Bar 1 moves down a string pair each beat; bar 2 comes back up from A and D to B and E.
Inside each loop every crossing is inside, as before. The move from one pair to the next (an upstroke, then a downstroke on the string below) is an outside crossing, so this one has both.
On G and B the lower string's upper note is fret 7, not 8: the box's shape changes there, the picking doesn't.
exercises.coachLine: The change of string pair is the risk. If a note goes missing, look at the beat it changed on.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: Four notes: B5-B8-e5-e8 in sixteenths
exercises.purpose: The four-note version, four to the click: one inside crossing and one outside in every loop, so it is the two kinds taking turns at speed.
howTo: Sixteenths. B string 5 and 8, top string 5 and 8, round again. Down, up, down, up.
Going up the crossing is inside (upstroke on B, downstroke on E); coming round from the top E's 8 to the B string's 5 it is outside.
exercises.coachLine: Faster than the six-note loop, and the turn back to the B string is the place to listen to.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: The mirror: the loop coming down
exercises.purpose: The six notes in reverse, from the top string's 8 down to the B string and back, and now every crossing is outside.
howTo: Sextuplets. Top string 8, 5, B string 8, 5, 8, top string 5, and round. Down, up, down, up, down, up.
If this one is clean and the first loop is not, your inside crossing is the weaker one: spend the extra minutes there.
exercises.coachLine: Compare this with the first loop. A big difference is worth knowing about.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

steps.title: Three notes per string
steps.goal: Run A minor in three-note-per-string shapes at sixteenths, where the crossing changes type at every string.
steps.why: An odd number of notes per string flips the stroke at each change, so outside and inside crossings take turns. This is the shape of most fast scalar playing: a long scale with no position shift to manage, and the same fingering idea on every string.
howTo: Each string has three notes, fretted 1-2-4 or 1-3-4 depending on the gaps. Open the hand from the first finger; don't twist the wrist to reach.
Sixteenths throughout, four to the click, so the string changes fall in different places in the beat. Count the beat, not the strings.
Ascending, the changes go outside, inside, outside. Say which one is next until you stop needing to.
steps.payoff: A two-and-a-half-octave A minor run, and a six-note lick you will use for the rest of your life.

exercises.title: The six-note lick, descending
exercises.purpose: C, B, A on the top string, then G, F, E on the B string, twice, landing on D. A real lick, with both crossings inside while it loops.
howTo: Sixteenths: the six notes twice (three beats), then a quarter note on the G string's fret 7. Little, middle, first finger on each string.
Starting on a downstroke, the change from the top string to the B string is inside both times. The landing note is a downstroke on the G string, an outside crossing.
exercises.coachLine: Even sixteenths first. This one is worth owning at a moderate tempo before it gets fast.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: The six-note lick, ascending
exercises.purpose: The mirror image, E, F, G then A, B, C, twice, landing on A: both crossings outside, so the two versions tell you which hop you own.
howTo: Sixteenths: the six notes twice, then a quarter note on the top string's fret 5. Starting on a downstroke, the pick stays outside the pair at each change.
exercises.coachLine: Compare this with the descending take. A big difference is worth a note in your practice.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: Three strings, up and down
exercises.purpose: Both kinds of crossing in one line, one straight after the other: nine notes up, seven back, one bar.
howTo: Sixteenths. From the start note, three notes on each of three strings going up, then back down without repeating the top note.
The first two strings use fingers 1, 3, 4 (a tone, then a tone); where a string has a semitone first, it is 1, 2, 4.
exercises.coachLine: When it is even both ways, the whole neck is the same idea with more strings.

exercises.title: Two and a half octaves at fifth position
exercises.purpose: The whole shape up and down in sixteenths, with the small hand shift where the top two strings move up a fret.
howTo: Sixteenths: eighteen notes up from the low E's fret 5, sixteen back down, and the A held to the end of bar 3.
The hand moves up one fret when you reach the B string, and back when you return to the G. Do it during the string change, not after it.

steps.title: Three-per-string sequences
steps.goal: Play A minor in groups of three, four and six, so the scale becomes phrases rather than a staircase.
steps.why: Nobody plays a scale straight up in a solo. Sequences are how a scale turns into lines: each group starts one note further on, and the ear hears the pattern rather than the notes. The group size is matched to the rhythm (threes as triplets, fours as sixteenths, sixes as sextuplets) so the group always starts on the beat.
howTo: Learn each sequence slowly by saying the first note of each group. If you lose the first note, you have lost the sequence.
Each Exercise names its rhythm: triplets are three to the click, sixteenths four, sextuplets six.
The fingering is the three-notes-per-string shape from the last Step. Don't change it to make a group easier.
steps.payoff: 'A minor in fours' up and down, and a six-note sequence in sextuplets that sounds like a real run.

exercises.title: Groups of three, as triplets
exercises.purpose: Three notes to the click, each group one scale note higher, up three strings and onto a landing.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets, three to the click: seven groups climbing, then a quarter note on the next string's first note.
Three is odd, so each group starts on the opposite stroke from the last. That is the point: the crossings keep changing.
exercises.coachLine: A long run like this usually slips in the same place. The evenness after the take helps you find it.

exercises.title: Groups of six, as sextuplets
exercises.purpose: Six notes to the click across four strings: four groups climbing in bar 1, four falling in bar 2. The shred sound, at a tempo where it is clean.
howTo: Sextuplets, six to the click. Bar 1 starts each group one note higher; bar 2 starts each group one note lower, from a note above where bar 1 ended.
Six is even, so every group starts on a downstroke. The string changes move around inside the beat.
exercises.coachLine: This is fast enough that the onset timing on a real rig is the weakest part of the reading, so trust your ear on the recording too.

exercises.title: Descending fours, onto a landing
exercises.purpose: Fours coming down three strings, then a half note: the descending sequence on its own, which most players find harder than the climb.
howTo: Sixteenths: six groups of four, each starting one scale note lower, then a half note two scale steps below where the run ends.
The landing is a downstroke after an even number of notes. Arrive on it exactly on beat 3.
exercises.coachLine: Land on time and the run was fine. I'll check the notes after the take.

steps.title: Speed bursts
steps.goal: Play short runs above your clean tempo and land on time, without tensing up for the whole bar.
steps.why: You can't practise speed by doing everything slowly and you can't do it by flailing. A burst is the honest middle: one beat of real speed, then a rest long enough that the hand lets go. Most players find a burst runs several rungs above what they can sustain, which tells them the wall is stamina or tension rather than how fast the fingers can go.
howTo: Rest between bursts. The rest is half the Exercise: let the hand go soft before the next one.
Aim at the landing note, not at the run. If you land on time, the run was fine.
Sixteenths in the bursts, sextuplets in the last one; the tempos here are well above the last Steps on purpose.
steps.payoff: You will hear yourself play a short run far faster than you thought you could, and it will be clean.

exercises.title: One beat on, one beat off
exercises.purpose: The shortest honest burst: four sixteenths and a quarter-note landing, twice a bar.
howTo: Four sixteenths with fingers 1-2-3-4, then a quarter note on the third finger. Everything relaxes during the quarter.
exercises.coachLine: Landing on time counts more than the run. Timing and missed notes are what I have here.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: Did the last note land with the click, and did the hand let go in the rest?

notPooled.reason: The frets get wider toward the nut, so a low position is harder than a high one.

exercises.title: Two beats on, two off
exercises.purpose: Twice the length with the same rest, so you find out how much of the speed survives eight notes.
howTo: Eight sixteenths up and back on one string, then a half note. The halfway point of the run is where the time usually moves.
exercises.coachLine: If one beat was clean and two is not, that is a stamina question and not a speed one.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: Expanding bursts
exercises.purpose: One beat, then two, three and four beats on: the classic way of walking a burst into a line.
howTo: Sixteenths. The bar tells you how long to keep going: bar 1 one beat, bar 2 two, bar 3 three, bar 4 no rest at all, so the hand has to stay loose while moving.
exercises.coachLine: Most people slip somewhere in the third bar. It helps to know which one is yours.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: The six-note burst, into a landing
exercises.purpose: Your descending six-note lick at sextuplet speed, then a walk down to A: this is how a fast run actually gets used in a solo.
howTo: One beat of sextuplets from the top string (C, B, A, G, F, E), then D, C and A as quarter notes. Land exactly on beat 2.
exercises.coachLine: Fast notes on a real rig are the hardest to time, so trust the landing and your own ear as much as the numbers.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: On a recording, can you still hear all six notes as six?

steps.difficultyException: The metric averages over the rests. Inside a burst the local rate is well above any earlier Step, which is the point.

steps.title: String skipping
steps.goal: Keep strict alternate picking going when the line jumps over a string, in octaves, pentatonics and a triad.
steps.why: So far every crossing has been to a neighbour. A skip makes the pick aim: it has to travel over a string it must not touch and arrive on time. Skipping is also where a lot of the modern shred sound comes from, because wide intervals on adjacent beats sound like nothing a scale can do.
howTo: On a skip, let the pick travel in a small arc over the string in between. Do not lift the whole forearm.
Mute the skipped string with the side of the picking hand and a spare fretting finger. Noise appears on skips before it appears anywhere else.
Sixteenths throughout.
steps.payoff: Octaves climbing the neck, a pentatonic line that leaps instead of walking, and an A minor triad that sounds like a sweep but is picked.

exercises.title: Octaves across a skipped string
exercises.purpose: Every pair is a skip and the same two fingers do all the fretting, so the aim is all that is left to practise.
howTo: Sixteenths, each octave twice. First finger on the lower string, third or little finger two strings up. Down on the low note, up on the high one: every crossing is outside.
A small shift each beat, up the scale in bar 1 and back in bar 2.
exercises.coachLine: If notes go missing here it is usually the skip or the shift. Slow down until neither is a surprise.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: The pentatonic box, skipping
exercises.purpose: Box 1 in pairs, every other pair a string further on: low E, D, A, G, D, B, G, E going up. It is the box you know, made to sound wide.
howTo: Sixteenths, two notes to a string. Bar 1 climbs: low E 5-8, D 5-7, A 5-7, G 5-7, D 7-5, B 5-8, G 7-5, top E 5-8. Bar 2 comes back down the same way.
Each pair is down-up, so every string change is a fresh downstroke after an upstroke.
exercises.coachLine: Skips are where noise starts. If extra notes show up in the report, the skipped string is the likely source.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: A minor over a skipped string
exercises.purpose: A, C on the D string, A, C on the B string, E on top, and back: an arpeggio with a skip in the middle, picked note by note.
howTo: Sixteenths, the eight notes twice a bar: D string 7 and 10, B string 10 and 13, top string 12, then B 13, B 10, D 10.
First finger on the D string's 7, then let the hand sit at fret 10: little finger for 13, ring for 12.
exercises.coachLine: I'll check the notes against the chord and the timing after the take.

steps.title: Economy picking
steps.goal: Alternate on a string, and let the pick carry straight through to the next string when it is already travelling that way.
steps.why: Strict alternate picking spends a stroke getting back over a string every time a three-note group changes string. Economy picking keeps going instead: the downstroke that ends one string falls through onto the next. Many shred players mix the two, and a five-note group is where economy picking shines, because the strokes come out the same on every repeat.
howTo: On one string, alternate. At a string change, if the next string is in the direction the pick is already moving, play it with the same stroke: one push, two strings.
The strokes are printed above the tab. The app cannot tell a downstroke from an upstroke, so each Exercise has a checklist question about them.
Don't let the push turn into a strum: the pick rests against the next string for an instant, then plays it, exactly in time.
steps.payoff: A three-string run that feels lighter than it did alternate-picked, and a five-note figure in quintuplets that rolls on its own.

exercises.title: Three per string, up: down-up-down, then through
exercises.purpose: Three strings up in A minor with the crossing downstroke carried through, one run a bar, from a different string each bar.
howTo: Sixteenths: nine notes up three strings, then rest for the remaining beat and three quarters. Strokes: down, up, down on each string, so each new string starts with a second downstroke that falls straight through from the last.
Bar 1 starts on the G string's fret 5, bar 2 the D string's, bar 3 the A string's, bar 4 the low E's, so each bar starts a string lower.
exercises.coachLine: I can check the notes and the timing. Whether the pick fell through or went round is on the checklist.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: Watch the pick for one bar, or film it: did each new string start with a downstroke that carried on from the last?

exercises.title: A five-note group in quintuplets
exercises.purpose: C, A on the top string, G, F, E on the B string: five notes to the click. With economy strokes the group starts on a downstroke every time, which is exactly why players use it.
howTo: Quintuplets: five notes to the click. Count 'one-two-three-four-five' evenly against the beat; it should feel slightly lopsided at first.
Top string 8, 5; B string 8, 6, 5. Strokes: down, up, then up again straight through to the B string, down, up. The next group's first note is a downstroke back onto the top string.
exercises.coachLine: Quintuplets are a feel thing, so the evenness bar here is a little looser. I'll check the notes after the take.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: Did every group of five start on a downstroke on the top string?

exercises.title: Three per string, down: up-down-up, then through
exercises.purpose: The mirror: three strings down, starting on an upstroke, so the upstroke that ends each string falls through to the string below.
howTo: Sixteenths: nine notes down three strings, then rest. Strokes: up, down, up on each string; each new string starts with a second upstroke.
Bar 1 comes down from the D string's fret 9 to the low E, bar 2 from the G string to the A, bar 3 from the B to the D, bar 4 from the top string to the G.
exercises.coachLine: Most players find this direction stickier. I'll check the notes and timing; the strokes are yours to check.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: Watch the pick for one bar: did each new string start with an upstroke carried on from the last?

exercises.title: Picked arpeggios: Am, F, C, G
exercises.purpose: Four-string arpeggios with strict alternate strokes, one chord a bar, for contrast: here every string change is picked, so you feel what economy saves and what it costs.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets, three to the click. Each bar is one chord, up and down twice. Am to F moves one note. Stay at fifth position.
These are alternate-picked, not swept: every stroke alternates even though the notes run across strings.
exercises.coachLine: I'll check the notes against the chords after the take. Whether it rings like a chord or sounds separated is yours to judge.

steps.difficultyException: Economy picking saves motion, so the note rate holds or drops. The new demand is the stroke plan, which no note-rate metric counts.

steps.title: Legato I: trills and pulls
steps.goal: Hammer-ons and pull-offs as loud and as even as picked notes, tied to a picked note on the beat.
steps.why: Legato is the other half of shred: the fretting hand plays most of the notes and the pick only marks the time. It sounds smooth only when the hammered notes are as strong as the picked ones, which is a strength and accuracy problem for the fretting hand. Every legato bar here comes after a picked bar of the same notes, so the picked bar sets the sound and the rhythm the legato bar has to match.
howTo: Hammer from a little height with the fingertip, and land exactly on the beat's subdivision. Pull off slightly sideways, toward the floor, so the string is plucked and not just released.
Keep the picked notes on the beat. They are what the timing is measured on most firmly.
Mute the strings you are not playing with the picking hand: legato rings the open strings more than picking does.
steps.payoff: A trill that sounds like one note shimmering, and a pentatonic waterfall of pull-offs in sextuplets.

exercises.title: Trill: picked, then hammered
exercises.purpose: Two notes a tone apart, sixteenths: one bar picked, one bar with only the first note of each beat picked and the rest hammered and pulled. Sixteen bars, for stamina in the fretting hand.
howTo: Sixteenths. Bar 1: alternate-pick G string 5, 7, 5, 7 for the whole bar. Bar 2: pick fret 5 on each beat with an accent, then hammer 7, pull to 5, hammer 7.
Fingers 1 and 3. The first finger stays down for the whole trill; only the third finger moves.
exercises.coachLine: Hammers and pulls I can't hear cost nothing here, so the picked notes carry the timing. Listen to the legato bar for volume.

notes: Hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides may be too quiet to detect. An unheard hammer-on or pull-off costs nothing. An unheard slid-to note still counts as missed today, so the bar here allows for it.

exercises.title: 5-7-8-7 on the top string, one pick a beat
exercises.purpose: A, B, C, B: three fingers, one string. One bar picked, then one bar where only the first note of each beat is picked and the other three are hammered and pulled.
howTo: Sixteenths. Bar 1: alternate-pick top string 5, 7, 8, 7 four times. Bar 2: pick 5 on each beat, hammer 7, hammer 8, pull to 7, and pick 5 again on the next beat.
The pull from 8 to 7 needs the second finger already down on 7. Place it while the 8 sounds.
exercises.coachLine: The picked notes on the beat are the anchor I time against most firmly. The volume of the legato notes is for your ear.

exercises.title: Pentatonic pull-offs in sextuplets
exercises.purpose: Down the box two strings at a time, a pull-off on every string: e 8 to 5, B 8 to 5, G 7 to 5. Bar 1 is picked, bar 2 picks only the upper note on each string.
howTo: Sextuplets, six to the click. Beats 1 and 2: top E, B and G strings; beats 3 and 4: B, G and D. Bar 1 picks every note. Bar 2 picks the upper note and pulls off to fret 5 on each string.
In bar 2 the picked notes alternate down, up, down across the strings.
exercises.coachLine: I'll check the notes where they are far enough apart to be sure of, and the timing. A pull-off I can't hear costs nothing.

steps.title: Legato II: three-per-string runs
steps.goal: Run three-note-per-string scales with one pick a string or less, hammering from nowhere going up and pulling off coming down.
steps.why: Three notes per string is where legato becomes a way to play scales fast with almost no picking. Going up, the first note of each new string has nothing to hammer from, so the finger hammers onto it from the air: the hammer-on from nowhere, and the skill that makes or breaks a legato run. Coming down, each string's first note is picked and the rest pulled.
howTo: Hammer-on from nowhere: the finger comes down hard and fast on the new string with no pick. The tab marks it T. It has to be loud, because there is no pick to help.
Sextuplets: six to the click, two strings to each beat.
Each Exercise is a picked bar, then the same notes legato. Match the legato bar to the picked one: same rhythm, same volume.
steps.payoff: Four strings of A minor at sextuplet speed with one picked note, and a lick you can play either way at will.

exercises.title: Up with hammers, from nowhere
exercises.purpose: Twelve notes up four strings, held at the top. Bar 1 picked; bar 2 picks the first note only, then hammers everything, the first note of each string from nowhere.
howTo: Sextuplets. Bar 1: alternate-pick the twelve notes from the low E's fret 5 up to the G string's fret 9 and hold the last one to the bar line. Bar 2: pick the first note, hammer the rest; on the A, D and G strings the first note is a hammer-on from nowhere (marked T).
Fingers 1-3-4 on the low E (5, 7, 8) and 1-3-4 on the A (5, 7, 8); 1-3-4 on the D and G (5, 7, 9).
exercises.coachLine: The hammer-ons from nowhere count as attacks here, so a quiet one shows up as missed. That is a fair reading of a hammer that didn't sound.

exercises.title: Down with pull-offs
exercises.purpose: The same twelve notes coming down. Bar 1 picked; bar 2 picks the first note on each string and pulls off the other two.
howTo: Sextuplets. Bar 1: alternate-pick from the G string's fret 9 down to the low E's fret 5 and hold it. Bar 2: pick 9 on the G string, pull to 7 and 5; pick 9 on the D, pull to 7 and 5; and so on down.
Have every finger of a string down before you pick its top note: you can only pull off to a note that is already fretted.
exercises.coachLine: The picked note on each string is the anchor. Pull-offs I can't hear cost nothing, so judge their volume by ear.

exercises.title: A picked bar, then a legato bar
exercises.purpose: The six-note lick (C, B, A, G, F, E) in sextuplets: four times picked, then four times with only the top note of each string picked. Same notes, two techniques, side by side.
howTo: Sextuplets. Bar 1: alternate-pick the lick four times. Bar 2: pick the top string's 8, pull to 7 and 5; pick the B string's 8, pull to 6 and 5.
Listen for the change at the bar line. If the legato bar is quieter or rushes, slow down until it doesn't.
exercises.coachLine: The picked bar is the one I can check most closely. The legato bar's volume is yours to judge against it.

steps.title: Sweep basics (timing only)
steps.goal: One continuous push of the pick through two and three strings, separate notes, nothing ringing, and a turn at the top.
steps.why: A sweep is one motion that plays several notes, which is why it is not alternate picking done faster. The smallest sweep, two strings, contains the whole technique and the whole problem: if the first note keeps ringing, you get a chord. The app grades these on timing only: swept notes ring into each other, so right notes mostly read 'not checked', and nothing here promises them.
howTo: One push from the arm, the wrist quiet. The pick comes to rest on the next string between notes, then falls through it.
Fretting hand: as soon as the next note sounds, release the last one without leaving the string. That is the mute that does most of the work.
Eighth-note triplets throughout, three to the click.
steps.payoff: A three-string A minor arpeggio that comes out of one stroke, turns at the top without a seam, and a two-string lick you can drop into a solo.

exercises.title: Two-string rolls (timing only)
exercises.purpose: Down through two strings at the same fret, rest, then up through them: the push, and the fingertip roll that keeps two notes from ringing.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets: two notes down, a rest, two notes up, a rest. One finger covers both strings and rolls so only the sounding note is pressed.
Down is one push through both strings; up is one pull back through them.
exercises.coachLine: Timing only: I can time the notes and say if one went missing or rang on as an extra. The roll is for your ear.

notes: Swept notes have soft attacks and can ring into each other. Detection of them is unproven, so only slow rungs are graded and the fast ones are self-checked.

selfCheck: Record a take and listen back. Does each note stop as the next one starts, or do they ring together like a strummed chord?
Between takes, stop and listen: are the strings you are not playing silent?

exercises.title: Am on three strings, both ways (timing only)
exercises.purpose: Up the A minor triad at fret 12 and back, with the top note as the only turn: the shape of a real sweep, slowly.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets: G string 14, B 13, top E 12, B 13, G 14, rest. Ring finger, middle, first.
The stroke changes once, right after the top note. Keep that change as small as you can.
exercises.coachLine: Timing only: right notes on a sweep mostly can't be checked, so I'm not claiming them. Evenness and missed notes I can give you.

exercises.title: The turnaround at fret 8 (timing only)
exercises.purpose: The whole loop: up three strings, a hammer to the top note and a pull back, down, and round with no extra stroke.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets, two loops a bar. On the Am shape: G string 9, B 10, top E 8, hammer to 12, pull to 8, B 10, and round. First finger on 8, second on 9, third on 10, little finger hammering 12.
After the top string's push the next note is a hammer, so the pick has nothing to do: use that moment to turn it round.
exercises.coachLine: Timing only. A quiet hammer or pull doesn't count against you, so don't dig in to please me.

exercises.purpose: Two-string sweeps with a hammer and a pull, ending on D: the Step's audible payoff, and a phrase that works in a solo.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets. Down through B and E at fret 5, hammer to 8, pull back to 5, then up through the B string's 8, pull to 5, and land on the G string's 7.
Only the unmarked notes are picked. The hammer and pulls give you notes for free.

steps.title: Five-string sweeps and links (timing only)
steps.goal: The classic five-string A minor sweep from fret 12, the link from one shape into the next, and Am, F, C, G one pass a chord.
steps.why: Five strings is the big sweep, the sound people mean by the word. It is only worth having if it connects: a progression doesn't wait while you find the next shape, so the link from one arpeggio into the next is practised as its own skill. As before, these are graded on timing only.
howTo: Mute everything. With five strings moving there is more to keep silent than there are fingers: palm on the low strings, fretting fingers across the high ones.
A link is one small move of the fretting hand on the top or bottom string: a hammer, a pull or a slide into the next chord's nearest note. The pick does nothing at that moment.
Eighth-note triplets for the loops; quarter-note triplets, three to every two clicks, for the one-pass progression.
steps.payoff: A five-string arpeggio up the neck and back with every note separate, and a four-chord progression played as one unbroken sweep.

exercises.title: A minor, the classic five-string shape (timing only)
exercises.purpose: A, C, E, A, C, E, A on five strings from the A string's fret 12, with a turn at each end. The most-used sweep shape there is.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets, one loop a bar. Hammer 12 to 15 on the A string at the bottom, one note a string up to the top, hammer and pull at the top, and down. The last note on the A string pulls off into the first note of the next loop.
exercises.coachLine: Timing only, and only up to the graded rungs. Above them the tempo is yours to judge on a recording.

exercises.title: The link: one shape into the next (timing only)
exercises.purpose: Two loops of one three-string shape, then two of the next, carried straight across the bar line: the link on its own, where it is easiest to hear.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets, two loops a bar. The upward push that finishes the last loop of bar 1 carries straight on into the first note of bar 2's shape: don't stop it and don't restart it.
Choose the nearest note of the new chord, not its root. Good links barely move the hand.
exercises.coachLine: Timing only. Listen for a gap at the bar line: it is the one thing a recording shows at once.

notes: Swept notes have soft attacks and can ring into each other. Detection of them is unproven, so only slow rungs are graded and the fast ones are self-checked.
Hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides may be too quiet to detect. An unheard hammer-on or pull-off costs nothing. An unheard slid-to note still counts as missed today, so the bar here allows for it.

selfCheck: At the bar line, did the sweep keep going, with no gap and no extra pick stroke before the new shape?
Record a take and listen back. Does each note stop as the next one starts, or do they ring together like a strummed chord?

exercises.title: Am, F, C, G: one pass a chord (timing only)
exercises.purpose: Up five strings on Am, link, down F, link, up C, link, down G: every chord change is a single small step on an outer string.
howTo: Quarter-note triplets, six notes a bar: one pass across five strings and one more note on the last string. The first note of each bar is a hammer, pull or slide from the last bar's final note, not a pick.
Sing the top notes if you can. They make a tune, and the tune is how you keep your place.
exercises.coachLine: Timing only. Four links a round; whether a link was picked is up to your ear.

notes: Swept notes have soft attacks and can ring into each other. Detection of them is unproven, so only slow rungs are graded and the fast ones are self-checked.
Hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides may be too quiet to detect. An unheard hammer-on or pull-off costs nothing. An unheard slid-to note still counts as missed today, so the bar here allows for it.

selfCheck: Record a take and listen back. Does each note stop as the next one starts, or do they ring together like a strummed chord?
Between takes, stop and listen: are the strings you are not playing silent?

exercises.title: Five-string loops in a chain (timing only)
exercises.purpose: One big loop to a chord through a minor progression, each shape starting as close as it can to the last, so most links are a fret or two.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets, one loop a bar. Watch the first note of each bar: it hardly moves, even though the chord does.
Where a top note is too wide to hammer, the tab slides to it. A slide is fine; the sound is what counts.
exercises.coachLine: Timing only. This is the big one: keep it where every note is separate.

steps.title: Tapping, then the etude
steps.goal: Tap a triplet arpeggio with the picking hand over the chords, hold a line for a minute, then play an eight-bar run over the band.
steps.why: Tapping adds notes no fretting hand could reach, and over chord changes it sounds bigger than anything else in this Path for the effort. Then the finale: a minute of unbroken sixteenths shows whether the speed is built on tension, and an eight-bar run with a band is the reason you did all the rest.
howTo: Tap with the middle finger of the picking hand, holding the pick tucked away. Tap hard and pull off slightly downward so the next note sounds. The tab marks a tap T.
Taps are the loud notes and the timing is read from them most firmly. The pulled and hammered notes between them may be too quiet to catch, and cost nothing if they are.
Stop at any pain in the hand, wrist or forearm. A tired forearm is one thing and pain is another; pain ends the set.
steps.payoff: A tapped arpeggio that moves with the chords, a full minute of sixteenths that sounds the same at the end as at the start, and an eight-bar run over a band.

exercises.title: Tap 12, pull to 5, hammer 8
exercises.purpose: The tapping cell: E tapped at fret 12, pull off to the A at 5, hammer the C at 8. Eighth-note triplets, one tap to every click.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets, three to the click. The fretting hand holds fret 5 with the first finger and hammers 8 with the little finger. The picking hand taps 12 on every click.
Mute the other strings with the side of the fretting hand's first finger.
exercises.coachLine: The taps carry the timing. Pull-offs and hammers I can't hear cost nothing.

notes: Hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides may be too quiet to detect. An unheard hammer-on or pull-off costs nothing. An unheard slid-to note still counts as missed today, so the bar here allows for it.

selfCheck: Was the pulled-off A as loud as the tapped E?

exercises.title: Tap, pull, hammer over Am, F and G
exercises.purpose: The same cell with the tap moving to each chord over a band: E for Am, F for F, G for G. The fretting hand moves only for the G.
howTo: Eighth-note triplets, one chord a bar. Am: tap 12, pull to 5, hammer 8. F: tap 13, pull to 5, hammer 8. G: tap 15, pull to 7, hammer 10, twice. Then round again.
Move the tap during the last hammer of the bar, so it lands on the next bar's first click.
exercises.coachLine: The taps carry the timing. With a band, direct input or headphones is the honest way to take this.

notes: Hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides may be too quiet to detect. An unheard hammer-on or pull-off costs nothing. An unheard slid-to note still counts as missed today, so the bar here allows for it.
With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

selfCheck: Did each tap land on the bar's first click when the chord changed?

exercises.title: The stamina minute
exercises.purpose: Three strings of A minor up and back, sixteenths, for sixty seconds without a stop, with both crossing types in every bar.
howTo: Sixteenths. Choose a rung about 20% below your clean tempo on three-per-string. It should feel slow for the first ten seconds.
Breathe. If the shoulder comes up, drop it during a bar line without stopping.
exercises.coachLine: If I stop catching notes on a long take, trust that report over your doubts about your hands. Long unbroken playing is something the listening has not been proven on.

notes: Long unbroken playing, especially high-gain, is where the onset noise floor may close and stop hearing you. Unproven either way; if the app says it did not catch enough, believe that before you doubt your hands.

exercises.title: The eight-bar run over the band
exercises.purpose: Eight bars of sixteenths over Am, F, C, G twice: the outside lick, a picked arpeggio, a C line, a scale run home, then the Gilbert four-note loop, an F line, the six-note lick and a run back to A.
howTo: Sixteenths throughout, one idea a bar, and every bar lands on a tone of its chord on beat 1. Play it dry first and hear that happen.
Listen to the snare, not to your own fingers. If you get lost, catch the next bar line and carry on.
Use direct input or headphones for a graded take: the band reaching a microphone has not been tested.
exercises.coachLine: This is the finale: sixteen bars, held to the end. Fast notes on a real rig are the hardest for me to place, so trust the evenness and your ear together.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

levels.title: Beginner: one string, then two
levels.summary: Sixteenths and sextuplets on one string, accents, the chromatic and spider drills, then crossings and the Gilbert pentatonic loops.

startHereIf: You can play eighth notes with a click at 90 BPM, but sixteenths come out uneven above about 90.
Your little finger is weaker than the others, or chromatic runs stumble at the B string.
Inside crossings, like the six-note loop on the top two strings, catch the pick.

warmups.title: A melody up one string
warmups.purpose: Sixteenths up one string in a minor key, a scale step higher each bar. A different string and key each time, so there is a tune to follow and a reason to move.
howTo: Sixteenths. Start well under your clean tempo. Follow the tune and let the hand travel with it.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

levels.title: Intermediate: scales, speed, skips and economy
levels.summary: Three notes per string and its sequences, speed bursts, string skipping, then economy picking and quintuplets.

startHereIf: You can hold even sixteenths on one string at about 110 BPM.
The six-note pentatonic loop is clean in sextuplets at about 85 BPM.
Scale runs across three strings fall apart, or you've hit a speed wall.

warmups.title: A scale in two positions
warmups.purpose: Three strings of a minor scale, up and back from two places on the neck, starting from a different root each time.
howTo: Sixteenths. Start well under your clean tempo. Change position at the bar line, and keep the shift small.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

levels.title: Advanced: legato, sweeps, tapping and the band
levels.summary: Legato tied to picked notes, sweeps graded on timing only, tapping over chords, a stamina minute and the eight-bar run.

startHereIf: You can run A minor three notes per string across three strings at sixteenths, 95 BPM.
Your picking is reliable and you want the fretting hand to do more of the work.
You've never swept, or your sweeps come out as a strummed chord.

warmups.title: The six-note loop around the chords
warmups.purpose: The Gilbert loop in sextuplets moved through i, iv and v of a minor key, on one of two string pairs, in a different key each time.
howTo: Sextuplets. Start well under your clean tempo. The hand moves at the bar line; the strokes don't change.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.
